title: What If a Tsunami Hit Britain? 8,200 Years Ago One Did, 20 Metres High

scenes.text: What if a tsunami hit Britain? One already did. It was 20 metres high.
About 8,200 years ago a chunk of seabed off Norway gave way: a landslide carrying 300 times the sediment all the world's rivers move in a year.
The Storegga slide shoved a wall of water across the North Sea. In Shetland, narrow valleys funnelled it up to 20 metres high.
On the British mainland the waves ran three to six metres, leaving sand layers in lakes and lagoons that geologists still dig up.
Stone Age people lived on that coast. Simulations suggest the wave could have wiped out much of the settlement at Howick, Northumberland.
Again? Younger tsunami sands, 5,000 and 1,500 years old, lie 13 metres above the sea in Shetland. It has happened more than once.

description:
What if a tsunami hit Britain? About 8,200 years ago one did: the Storegga submarine landslide off Norway sent waves across the North Sea that reached about 20 metres high in Shetland.
The slide moved roughly 300 times the sediment carried each year by all the world's rivers combined. Waves on the British mainland are estimated at about 3 to 6 metres, leaving sand layers in lakes and lagoons; a 2024 modelling study suggests the tsunami could have devastated the Mesolithic settlement at Howick, Northumberland. Later tsunami deposits in Shetland, about 5,000 and 1,500 years old, lie up to 13 metres above sea level.
